content:
Earlier this year, I replaced my battery-powered push mower with an iPhone-controlled robotic mower. You can manually drive it around your yard to build a virtual map, and once set up, it automatically handles mowing on a schedule.

Recently, I have been testing another system called the TerraMow V1000. It uses a completely different navigation method, and after several weeks of testing, I believe it may be a more approachable option for many people.

Camera-driven automatic mapping

The biggest difference between the TerraMow V1000 and the Anthbot M9 I reviewed earlier this year lies in how each machine understands your yard.

The Anthbot M9 uses an RTK base station for positioning. During setup, I had to manually drive the mower along the boundaries with my iPhone to create an initial map.

The TerraMow V1000, on the other hand, uses a system the company calls TerraVision 2.0. It has three built-in cameras that let the mower automatically map your lawn without needing buried boundary wires or a separate RTK antenna.

Automatic mapping took longer to build my initial map. But I think it may be easier for people who are less tech-savvy and don't enjoy "fiddling around."

To test this idea, I had my mother, who lives in another state, set up and use the TerraMow V1000 on her own without my help. She reported that everything worked well. However, I'm not sure she would have had the patience to first manually remote-control the robot around the entire boundary and then individually mark off zones to avoid.

Automatic mapping did create one minor quirk in my front yard. Since there's no fence or physical separation between my lawn and my neighbour's, the TerraMow initially incorporated part of my neighbour's grass into my map as well.

I corrected this by marking the area as a no-go zone in the app. This shows that if there's no clear visual boundary between lawns, you may need to pay extra attention during the initial mapping process.

A peek through the mower's cameras

TerraMow's cameras also support one of my favourite features. The iPhone app can show a live view of what the mower sees while it's working.

During testing, I used the iPhone Mirroring feature on my Mac to keep the feed open in a large window. I could work indoors while watching the mower move around the backyard from its perspective.

This feature isn't necessary for automatic mowing, but it makes the robot more engaging, and occasionally helps explain why it slows down or avoids certain obstacles. The Anthbot M9 does not offer a similar camera view.

The two iPhone apps share a lot in common in other respects. Both let you schedule jobs, adjust mowing settings, create zones, mark no-go areas, and remote-control the mower.

TerraMow has a particularly clever design for that last feature. In addition to the traditional left/right virtual joysticks, its app offers a single-handed joystick mode. You can hold your iPhone normally and guide the mower with your thumb.

Manually driving the mower with your iPhone isn't the main purpose of either system. Ideally, the robot should run automatically on a schedule without any intervention. However, TerraMow's joystick control is excellent for cleaning up missed spots.

Sometimes, I almost feel like I'm operating the robot by telepathy (and it's a pleasant feeling). I can walk alongside the mower with my iPhone held low, making only slight movements with my thumb, and the machine follows my direction.

Every robotic mower app should copy this control method.

More aggressive mowing performance

The TerraMow V1000 also feels more aggressive than the Anthbot M9. In my testing, it cut lower and was louder while operating.

I wouldn't call the TerraMow noisy, but the difference between the two is noticeable. The Anthbot is extremely quiet in operation, making it easy to forget it's working—even when it's mowing after dark using its headlights.

Since TerraMow relies on cameras for navigation, it needs daylight to operate reliably. This makes daytime scheduling more important.

The V1000 itself feels solid and sturdy, and is also larger than the Anthbot M9. TerraMow includes a protective garage in the box to cover the charging dock, whereas the Anthbot's garage must be purchased separately.

Most importantly, the TerraMow performed consistently and reliably. I relied on it for weeks on end without needing to take over the routine mowing myself.

When adaptive mapping is too "clever"

The same visual intelligence that makes TerraMow easy to set up can sometimes backfire.

The mower continuously adjusts its map based on what it sees. After each session, saving these changes takes some time, during which you temporarily can't perform other operations in the app.

After several days of heavy rain, I encountered an interesting edge case. Water pooled in parts of the yard, and the TerraMow reasonably avoided those areas on its next run.

Inside the skipped circles, the grass subsequently grew taller. Over time, the mower seemed to interpret this growth as a zone to keep avoiding, leaving it uncut even after the ground dried.

I eventually used the app's remote-control function to manually drive the mower through that taller patch of grass. Once the area returned to normal lawn condition, the automatic mowing resumed working normally.

Regular edge trimming also helps the TerraMow reach boundaries smoothly. Tall grass growing along indistinct dividing lines might otherwise be mistaken for obstacles rather than part of the mowing area.

By comparison, Anthbot's approach feels less adaptive. It relies more on the boundaries and obstacles you set yourself. This requires more work upfront, but it also avoids the map "changing its mind" about a patch of grass.

9to5Mac's take

After trying both systems, for most people, I lean toward recommending TerraMow's camera-based approach.

Burying boundary wires is completely impractical for me, and installing an RTK base station means yet another piece of hardware I have to place, power, and maintain. TerraMow requires neither.

Its visual navigation isn't flawless. The initial mapping takes longer, an invisible property line needed manual correction, and its adaptive behaviour once mistook overgrown weeds for permanent obstacles.

These issues are all manageable. In return, the TerraMow V1000 offers simpler setup, reliable automatic mowing, an engaging live camera view, and the best robotic mower app manual control experience I've used.

I genuinely enjoy working in the garden, but mowing is the most repetitive part. Handing it off to a robot frees up more time for landscaping, trimming, and detail work, while keeping the lawn looking tidy.

The TerraMow V1000 is more than capable of handling the job, and I'd recommend it—especially for those who want to skip burying wires, installing an RTK antenna, or manually walking the entire yard with an iPhone.

Currently, the TerraMow V1000 is priced at $999 on Amazon, available after applying a $200 coupon on the site. You can also purchase it from TerraMow's official website.
